Paint only lasts as long as the wood under it

Most of a historic repaint happens before the first coat. Each house on this row is a job we see every week, and the repair it needs first.

  • Church Street porch Peeling at the sills Hand-scrape and prime

  • Sullivan's Island rail Salt-softened balusters Wood and trim repair

  • Twelve shutters Louvers painted shut Stripped in our shop

  • Front gate More rust than iron Wire-brush, metal primer

Low-country humidity sets the schedule.

We start when the dew burns off and stop before it settles back.

House 06 · The piazza

Haint blue that stays clean

The pale blue porch ceilings Charleston is known for turn gray with mildew every summer when the prep is rushed. Ours go on in four steps.

  1. 01Mildew Black spots by July: spores living in the old coat.
  2. 02Wash Low-pressure wash and a mildewcide rinse, every board.
  3. 03Prime Mildew-resistant primer, dried a full day.
  4. 04Two coats Haint blue, brushed into each bead.

“Our single house on Tradd Street hadn't been painted in eleven years. Wendell's crew replaced six rotten balusters, hand-scraped the piazza and matched the old yellow from a chip they took under the eaves. It looks like the house in the 1950s photo we have.”

Eleanor G. · Charleston · Historic exterior repaints · 5 of 5 Sample review

“The porch ceiling had black mildew spots every summer. They washed it, used a mildew-resistant primer and repainted it pale blue. Two summers now and it is still clean.”

Marcus J. · Mount Pleasant · 5 of 5 Sample review

“We live on the marsh on James Island and the paint used to chalk off within three years. They explained why they wanted to start early in the morning and stop when the dew came back. So far so good.”
